A says 'only one movement' can help, as if voters were sure. B says 'nobody else is doing anything, so let them try', which shows he chose them with little faith. They also differ in purpose. A was written by the Nazis to win votes before an election, so it blames 'the parties of the Republic' and makes a big promise. B is a worker looking back many years later to explain his own choice. He has nothing to sell, so he admits he 'did not care much about politics'.

It does not say why Hitler's opponents failed to stop him. Source D fills that gap: the Social Democrats and the Communists 'never joined hands'. C can be trusted for what it does say. It is a historian writing sixty years later with no side to defend, and its point that 'the Nazi vote fell' fits D, which says the two parties together 'had more seats than the Nazis'. So C is very useful for the last step, the appointment, but not for the whole story.

Source A shows the Nazis used the Depression to win votes: 'Six million Germans have no work' and they promise 'work and bread'. Source B agrees. The worker was 'out of work for two years' and so he decided to 'let them try'. Source C disagrees. It says the Depression 'did not give him power': a small group 'persuaded the President to appoint him'. Source D also disagrees. It says the Republic fell 'because its defenders were divided'. The sources that disagree are stronger. A is a leaflet meant to win votes, and B is one worker. C is a historian with the whole picture and no side to defend, and its point that 'the Nazi vote fell' shows the Depression alone was not enough. D defends his own party, but he admits its mistake, which makes him more believable. So I agree only to some extent: the Depression gave Hitler his support, but the deal that made him Chancellor was the deciding step.

People in Britain felt relieved that war had been avoided. The source says that a week before, families were 'fitting gas masks on their children', but now 'those children can sleep'. This shows people had truly expected to be bombed, so the agreement felt like an escape from danger.

They also differ in whose side they take. A was written for American readers and praises the President, who 'stood firm'. B was written for Soviet readers and makes the removal look like a choice, not a retreat. Each wants its own people to believe their leader won.

It is useful. It shows that the Soviet Union backed down in public: 'The Soviet ships turned back' and the missiles are 'being crated and shipped home'. It is limited. It tells us only what the Soviet Union gave up. Source C shows the United States gave something too: it 'promised not to invade' and 'Secretly' agreed to remove its missiles from Turkey. A's writer could not know this, because that part 'was kept from the public for many years'. A is also an American magazine cheering its own President, so it calls the result 'a clear victory'. It is useful for how the ending looked to Americans in 1962, not for what was really agreed.
